title: Project+ V5 (PK0-005) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public PK0-005 exam objectives. Not real exam questions.

q.q: Which of these is a project rather than ongoing operations?
o: Running the nightly backup job for the file servers
Monitoring the network operations center's alerts all year
Resetting user passwords at the help desk every day
Replacing every switch in a building by March
Right. It's temporary and creates a unique result, with a start and finish.

q.q: A unit runs several related projects (new radios, new towers, new training) managed together for a shared goal. What is this group called?
o: A portfolio is all the projects and programs an organization runs, related or not.
A single project with three phases
These are separate projects with their own scopes.
Right. A program groups related projects to get benefits they couldn't deliver alone.
An operations plan for the year
Operations are ongoing, not a set of projects.

q.q: A team uses a board with To do, Doing and Done columns, limits work in progress and has no fixed-length iterations. Which method is this?
o: Waterfall runs phases in order, not a continuous board.
Right. Kanban visualizes flow and limits work in progress without fixed sprints.
PRINCE2 is a stage-based governance method.

q.q: A team adds security checks into every stage of its automated build and release pipeline. Which approach is this?
o: Waterfall with a security phase at the end
That's security as a late, separate phase.
XP focuses on engineering practices like pair programming.
SAFe scales agile across teams; it isn't specifically about security in the pipeline.
Right. DevSecOps builds security into the DevOps pipeline instead of at the end.

q.q: A data center move has a fixed date, a fixed budget and requirements that are clear and won't change. Which approach fits best?
o: XP is a software development method.
Right. Clear, stable requirements and fixed constraints suit a planned, phased approach.
Agile shines when requirements are uncertain.
Kanban with no planned end date
The move has a fixed date and scope.

q.q: Users can't describe what a new internal app should look like until they see something working. Which approach fits best?
o: Skip requirements and build everything at once
Waterfall, with all requirements signed off first
Users can't give final requirements up front.
Agile, with short iterations and demos
Right. Frequent working increments let users react and refine requirements.
A fixed-price contract for the full app

q.q: In Scrum, who decides the order of the product backlog?
o: The project sponsor in every sprint
The sponsor funds and supports; the product owner prioritizes.
Right. The product owner owns the backlog and its priority.
The development team's most senior engineer
The team estimates and builds; it doesn't own priority.
The Scrum master coaches the process and removes blockers.

q.q: A stakeholder asks for a new report feature halfway through the project. What should the project manager do first?
o: Log a change request and assess its impact
Right. Changes go through the change control process before anyone acts.
Add it quietly and absorb the extra time
Tell the team to add it since the stakeholder is important
Refuse it because the scope is already approved
Changes can be approved; they just need the process.

q.q: After the change control board approves a change, which step comes next?
o: Close the change request and let the requester tell the team
The team and stakeholders need to know.
Ask the requester to submit it again
Update the project plan and baselines, then communicate the change
Right. Approved changes must be reflected in the plan and shared.
Start the work without updating the schedule
The plan would no longer match reality.

q.q: Small features keep getting added through hallway conversations, and the project is now late. What is this problem?
o: Fast tracking runs tasks in parallel.
Gold plating is the team adding extras nobody asked for.
Right. Uncontrolled additions to scope without process.
Crashing adds resources to shorten the schedule.

q.q: A key vendor might go out of business. The team signs a backup vendor in advance. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer shifts the impact to a third party, like insurance.
Avoiding would mean not using the vendor at all.
Accepting means doing nothing ahead of time.
Right. Lining up a backup reduces the impact if the risk happens.

q.q: There's a chance a new tool will be released early, which would let the project finish sooner. The PM assigns someone to track it and be ready to adopt it. What is this?
o: Right. Enhance raises the chance or benefit of a positive risk.
Mitigating a threat to the schedule
This is a positive risk, not a threat.
Nothing is shifted to a third party.

q.q: Where does a project manager record each risk, its owner, probability, impact and planned response?
o: Issues have already happened; risks might happen.
Right. The register tracks every identified risk and its response.
The charter authorizes the project and lists high-level risks only.

q.q: A risk has a 20% chance of happening and would cost $50,000. What is its expected monetary value?
o: Right. EMV = probability x impact = 0.20 x 50,000.
That's the full impact, ignoring probability.

q.q: A server shipment arrived damaged, delaying installation. This has already happened. Where should it be tracked?
o: That says how to communicate, not what's going wrong.
That's for reflection, not active tracking.
The risk register, as a new high-probability risk
The issue log, with an owner and due date
Right. Issues are problems that are happening now.

q.q: The same network outage hits the project lab three times. What should the PM do beyond restoring service?
o: Add a new risk to the register and close it
It's an active issue, not a risk.
Run a root cause analysis and fix the underlying cause
Right. Repeated issues need their cause found so they stop.
Restore service faster each time with a written workaround

q.q: An issue is beyond the project manager's authority to resolve. What is the right next step?
o: Tell the team to work around it forever
A workaround may help short term but needs a decision.
Resolve it anyway and explain the decision to leadership later
Escalate it through the defined escalation path
Right. The issue goes to someone with authority, as planned.
Ignore it until the end of the project

q.q: Task B can't start until task A finishes. Which dependency is this?
o: The successor can't finish until the predecessor starts.
Right. The most common type: the successor starts after the predecessor finishes.

q.q: Paths through a project take 18, 22 and 25 days. What is the critical path duration?
o: That's a middle path with slack.
Right. The critical path is the longest path; it sets the shortest possible project length.
Paths run in parallel; you don't add them.

q.q: A task on the critical path slips by two days, and nothing else changes. What happens to the project end date?
o: Critical path tasks have no float.
Right. Critical tasks have zero float, so any delay delays the project.
It moves out by four days
It moves in by two days
A delay can't make the project shorter.

q.q: The schedule is behind. The PM adds two more engineers to critical tasks, at extra cost. What technique is this?
o: Leveling smooths resource use and can lengthen the schedule.
Right. Adding resources to shorten the schedule, usually at a cost.
That resets the baseline; it doesn't shorten the schedule.
Fast tracking overlaps tasks instead of adding people.

q.q: A project has spent $120,000. The work completed was budgeted at $100,000. What is the cost variance?
o: That's the actual cost, not the variance.
Spending more than earned is a variance.

q.q: Before release, real users try the new system to confirm it meets their needs. Which test is this?
o: Right. End users confirm the system meets requirements.
A quick check that the basics work after a build.

q.q: After a bug fix, the team re-runs old tests to make sure nothing else broke. What is this?
o: Right. Checks that existing features still work after a change.

q.q: Schedule performance index (SPI) is 0.8. What does it mean?
o: The project is exactly on track
Right. SPI below 1 means less work was done than planned.
The project is ahead of schedule

q.q: Team members are spread across time zones nine hours apart. Which approach helps most?
o: Daily meetings at 8 a.m. in the PM's time zone, required for every member
That's midnight for some members every day.
Asynchronous updates with a shared written record, plus a rotating meeting time
Right. Written, async updates reach everyone; rotating meetings share the burden.
Phone calls only, with no notes
Leaves no record and needs everyone awake.
Wait until everyone is in the same time zone

q.q: The communication plan says the sponsor gets a one-page status every two weeks. The sponsor now wants a weekly dashboard. What should the PM do?
o: Update the communication plan and deliver the dashboard
Right. Plans change when stakeholder needs change.
Keep sending the biweekly report since the plan says so
Send every team email to the sponsor instead
Too much detail for a sponsor.
Stop reporting until the next phase

q.q: Which communication is formal and external?
o: A chat message to a teammate
A hallway conversation with the sponsor
A signed letter to a vendor about contract terms
Right. It's official and goes outside the organization.
An internal team stand-up about the vendor contract

q.q: Daily stand-ups keep running 45 minutes because people solve problems in them. What should the Scrum master do?
o: Make them longer so every problem gets solved while everyone is there
That wastes the whole team's time.
Hold them once a month instead
Timebox the stand-up and move problem-solving to a follow-up
Right. Stand-ups are short status syncs; deep discussions happen after.

q.q: Who records decisions and action items during a meeting?
o: The facilitator while also running the meeting
Possible, but the facilitator's focus is guiding the meeting.
Right. The scribe captures minutes and action items.
The most junior attendee by default
The role is assigned, not by rank.

q.q: At the end of a sprint, the team shows the working increment to stakeholders for feedback. Which meeting is this?
o: Right. The review shows the work and gathers feedback.
Planning picks work for the next sprint.
The retro looks at how the team worked, not the product.

q.q: A new project team argues about roles and how to work together in its second week. Which stage is this?
o: Norming is when the team agrees on how to work.
Right. Conflict about roles and methods is the storming stage.
Forming is the polite, getting-to-know-you stage.
Adjourning is when the team disbands.

q.q: Team members report to their functional managers but also work for the project manager, who shares authority with them. Which structure is this?
o: Right. Authority is shared between functional and project managers.
Not one of the standard project structures.
In a projectized structure the PM has full authority.
In a functional structure the PM has little authority.

q.q: Two projects need the same network engineer in the same week. What is the PM's best move?
o: Raise the resource conflict with the managers and agree on priority
Right. Shared resources need a decision by those who set priorities.
Hire a new engineer without approval
Book the engineer on both projects and ask them to work extra hours

q.q: Who provides funding for the project and champions it with leadership?
o: Right. The sponsor funds, supports and removes high-level obstacles.
The Scrum master coaches the team.

q.q: A unit knows exactly what equipment it needs and wants vendors to send prices only. Which document should it issue?
o: An RFI gathers general information when needs are unclear.
An RFP asks vendors to propose how they'd solve a problem.
Right. An RFQ asks for pricing on a clearly defined need.

q.q: The work is unclear and may change, so the buyer wants to pay for hours worked plus materials. Which contract type fits?
o: That reimburses costs plus a performance incentive, usually for large, uncertain work.
Right. The buyer pays for actual hours and materials as the work evolves.
A purchase order for a fixed quantity

q.q: Which document describes the specific work, deliverables and timeline a vendor will provide?
o: Right. The SOW defines what the vendor will do and deliver.
The MSA sets general terms for future work.

q.q: Before a project is approved, leadership wants to know the expected benefits, costs and return. Which document provides this?
o: The charter comes after approval to authorize the project.
The WBS breaks down approved scope.
Right. It justifies the project with benefits, costs and ROI.

q.q: A project buys servers (owned for years) and also pays a monthly cloud subscription. How are these usually classed?
o: Owned servers are usually capital assets.
Servers as CapEx, the subscription as OpEx
Right. Long-lived assets are capital expenses; recurring services are operating expenses.
Servers as OpEx, the subscription as CapEx

q.q: Early in discovery, the team documents how the help desk works today and how it should work after the new ticketing system. What is this?
o: A risk register with each process gap listed
A current state and future state assessment
Right. Comparing the two shows the gap the project must close.

q.q: During discovery, the PM checks whether the organization already has contracts with vendors who could do the work. Why?
o: Because new vendors are never allowed
New vendors are allowed through procurement.
Because existing vendors always cost the least and need no new paperwork
Using existing contracts or prequalified vendors can save time
Right. Procurement is faster when vendors are already vetted.
To skip writing a scope statement

q.q: A project costs $200,000 and is expected to return $260,000 in benefits. What is the ROI?
o: That divides the gain by the benefits, not the cost.
That's the gain divided by $100,000, not the cost.
That's benefits divided by cost, without subtracting the cost.

q.q: Which belongs in discovery rather than planning?
o: Building the detailed schedule and resource plan
Deciding whether the project is worth doing at all
Right. Discovery explores the idea and its value before committing.

q.q: Which document formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority to use resources?
o: Right. The charter authorizes the project and names the PM.
The business case justifies it; the charter authorizes it.

q.q: A RACI chart lists 'Approve the cutover plan' with one person as A. What does A mean?
o: Accountable: the one person who owns the outcome and signs off
Right. Each task has exactly one accountable person.
Aware: someone who is told about it
Assigned: the person who does the hands-on work for the task

q.q: What is the main goal of a project kickoff meeting?
o: Approve the final deliverables and release the project budget
Align everyone on goals, roles, scope and how the team will work
Right. The kickoff starts the project with shared understanding.

q.q: During initiation, the PM learns the team will need badges and accounts on a secure network before work can start. Where should this be captured?
o: Nowhere; the team will figure it out
Delays work when access is missing.
As access requirements in the initiation documents
Right. Access needs are identified early so they don't delay execution.
In the lessons learned register, to note for the next project
That's for reflection, not planning access.

q.q: Who should be identified first so the project knows whose needs and influence matter?
o: Right. A stakeholder register lists everyone affected and their influence.

q.q: A charter lists 'success criteria'. What is an example?
o: Use the newest laptop model available
That's a preference, not a measure of success.
Hold a status meeting with the sponsor every Monday at 9 a.m.
All 400 laptops replaced by June 30 with less than 2% help desk tickets
Right. Success criteria are measurable conditions for success.

q.q: The PM breaks the project's deliverables into smaller pieces down to work packages. What is this?
o: Right. The WBS decomposes scope into manageable work packages.
A Gantt chart of every task
A Gantt chart shows tasks on a timeline.

q.q: Once the scope, schedule and budget are approved, they become the reference used to measure progress. What are they called?
o: Milestones are key points in the schedule.
Right. Baselines are approved versions used to measure variance.
Assumptions are things believed true for planning.

q.q: Which plan explains how the finished system will be handed over to the operations team?
o: That covers buying goods and services.
That covers who gets what information.
Right. It covers handoff, training, support and documentation for operations.

q.q: A scope statement includes 'Out of scope: printer replacement.' Why list exclusions?
o: To prevent misunderstandings and scope creep
Right. Saying what's not included sets clear expectations.
To assign the printers to the sponsor
To give the sponsor a list of future project ideas
Exclusions set limits on this project; they aren't a wish list.
Because printers are never part of IT projects

q.q: In agile planning, what replaces a detailed WBS for the whole project?
o: Right. Agile teams keep an ordered backlog that changes over time.
A fixed scope statement signed at the start
Not a planning tool for scope.

q.q: The PM estimates a task three ways: optimistic 4 days, most likely 6, pessimistic 14. Using the PERT formula, what is the estimate?
o: That's the most likely value alone.
That's the average of optimistic and pessimistic.
That's the simple average of the three.

q.q: A new ticketing system is live, but staff keep using email instead. What should the PM focus on?
o: Organizational change: training, communication and support for adoption
Right. People need help changing how they work.
Turning off email for the whole company
Adding more features to the new system so it beats email
The issue is adoption, not features.
Closing the project since the system is live

q.q: Two senior engineers disagree strongly about the design, and work has stalled. Which conflict approach usually gives the most lasting result?
o: Smoothing it over by focusing on agreement only
Collaborating to find a solution both accept
Right. Problem-solving together addresses the real issue.
Avoiding the topic until it goes away

q.q: At the end of the design phase, leadership reviews progress before allowing the build phase to start. What is this?
o: Right. A go/no-go checkpoint between phases.

q.q: A vendor keeps missing delivery dates in the SOW. What should the PM do first?
o: Hire a new vendor without telling procurement
Ignore it since the vendor is cheap
Stop paying all invoices until the vendor catches up
Unilateral action may breach the contract.
Review performance against the contract and address it with the vendor
Right. Vendor management uses the agreed terms.

q.q: During execution, how does the PM know if the project is on budget?
o: The business case is a forecast.
Ask each team lead whether they think they're on budget
Track actual costs against the cost baseline
Right. Comparing actuals to the baseline shows variance.

q.q: The system is delivered. What must happen before the project is closed?
o: Keep vendor contracts open just in case
Start the next project immediately with the same team
Formal acceptance and sign-off of the deliverables
Right. The customer or sponsor confirms the deliverables meet requirements.

q.q: A contractor's project ends. What access step belongs in closing?
o: Remove the contractor's accounts, badges and system access
Right. Access granted for the project must be revoked.
Leave access on in case of future work
Unused access is a security risk.
Leave the access on for 90 days in case of warranty work
Share one account for any follow-up

q.q: Where does the team record what went well and what to do differently next time?
o: Right. Lessons learned help future projects.

q.q: Which belongs in the project closeout report?
o: The original sales pitch from the vendor
Final scope, schedule and budget results compared with the baselines
Right. The report summarizes how the project performed.
Daily stand-up notes from every sprint, attached in full

q.q: After sign-off, the team still has engineers assigned to the project. What should the PM do?
o: Release resources back to their managers
Right. Releasing resources is part of closing.
Assign them to new scope without approval
Keep them on the project's budget for a month
Delete their accounts on every system

q.q: A project is canceled midway. Should closing activities still happen?
o: Records, contracts and lessons still matter.
Contracts, access and records do too.
Yes: document status, close contracts, archive records and capture lessons learned
Right. Canceled projects still need formal closure.
Only if the sponsor asks for a formal report on the canceled work

q.q: Which chart shows tasks as bars on a timeline, with dependencies and progress?
o: Right. Gantt charts show tasks, durations and dependencies over time.
Shows the relationship between two variables.

q.q: Which tool links each requirement to the design, build and test items that cover it?
o: Right. It traces each requirement through to delivery and testing.

q.q: Which diagram shows task order and dependencies as boxes and arrows, used to find the critical path?
o: Right. Network diagrams map task order to calculate the critical path.

q.q: Testers find faults in the new app. Where are these tracked until fixed?
o: Right. Defects are tracked with severity, owner and status.

q.q: Leadership wants a one-glance view of schedule, budget and risk health for five projects. What should the PM give them?
o: Right. Dashboards summarize key measures visually.
The full WBS and task list for every project

q.q: Which chart shows only the key events and dates, like 'Design approved' and 'Go live'?
o: Shows completed work against total scope.
Shows whether a process is stable.
Right. It highlights key points without every task.

q.q: An agile team moves cards between To do, In progress and Done on a shared board. What tool is this?
o: Right. It visualizes work and its status.
A Gantt chart of every task

q.q: A distributed team needs to edit the same requirements document at the same time. Which tool type fits?
o: Right. Several people edit one file together.
Email attachments sent back and forth with version numbers

q.q: Users report problems with the new system. Which tool tracks each request from report to resolution?
o: Right. Tickets track requests, owners and status.

q.q: The team wants to find a meeting time across time zones without emailing back and forth. Which tool fits?
o: A shared calendar or scheduling tool
Right. Shows availability and books the slot.

q.q: A project handles sensitive data. The team wants to choose between cloud-based and on-premises collaboration tools. What should drive the decision?
o: Security, compliance and data handling requirements
Right. Where data may live and who can access it decide the fit.
Whichever tool the team already uses on personal accounts
Personal accounts may not meet the data handling rules.
Always on-premises, because cloud is never allowed
Cloud tools can meet many requirements.
Whatever the newest team member used at their last job

q.q: Quick questions between team members keep getting lost in long email threads. What helps most?
o: A team chat channel for informal, quick communication
Right. Chat suits quick, informal back-and-forth.
A change request for each question
A formal monthly report that lists every open question

q.q: Which tool would a PM use to build budget calculations and track cost totals?
o: Right. Spreadsheets handle formulas and totals.

q.q: The team records meetings for members who can't attend live. Which communication type does the recording support?
o: Right. People consume it later, not at the same time.
Synchronous means at the same time.

q.q: The help desk wants to find the few causes behind most tickets so it can fix those first. Which chart helps?
o: Right. Bars sorted by frequency with a cumulative line show the vital few causes (80/20).

q.q: A process measure stays within upper and lower limits except for one point far outside. Which chart shows this?
o: Right. Control charts show whether a process is stable and flag outliers.

q.q: The team wants to brainstorm possible causes of slow deployments, grouped by people, process, tools and environment. Which diagram fits?
o: Shows a relationship between two variables.
Right. It organizes possible causes by category.

q.q: A burndown chart shows the remaining-work line flat for the last five days of the sprint. What does it suggest?
o: The chart is a Pareto chart
Work isn't being completed, so the sprint may miss its goal
Right. A flat line means remaining work isn't going down.
The team finished early and stopped updating the chart

q.q: A team completes 20, 24 and 22 story points in three sprints. Which chart shows this, and what is the average?
o: A velocity chart; about 22 points per sprint
Right. Velocity charts show work completed per sprint. (20+24+22)/3 = 22.
A Pareto chart; 24 points per sprint
24 is the best sprint, not the average.
A burndown chart; 66 points per sprint on average
66 is the total, not the average.
A Gantt chart; 20 points per sprint

q.q: Which chart helps the PM see if longer meetings relate to more defects?
o: Right. It plots two variables to show a relationship.

q.q: The PM must choose between two vendors, each with chances of delay and different costs. Which tool shows the expected value of each choice?
o: Right. Branches show choices, probabilities and expected outcomes.

q.q: A hardware refresh will retire 600 old laptops. Which ESG concern should the plan address?
o: Shortening the schedule so users get new laptops sooner
Schedule speed isn't the environmental question here.
Holding more status meetings with the vendor
Meetings are communication, not environmental impact.
Choosing the fastest laptops the budget allows
Performance is a technical choice, not an ESG concern.
Responsible disposal and recycling of the old equipment
Right. Environmental impact is part of ESG.

q.q: A project could cut costs by using a vendor known for labor violations. Which ESG factor applies?
o: Right. How the work affects people and the brand matters.

q.q: Why might a data center project choose a site powered by renewable energy, even at slightly higher cost?
o: Because a renewable site always finishes construction faster
Power source doesn't set the construction schedule.
Because renewable energy always costs less
Because renewable power removes the need for backup generators
Sites still need backup power for outages.
To meet environmental goals and regulations the organization has set
Right. ESG commitments can shape project choices.

q.q: A new app will collect data in ways that could hurt public trust if reported in the news. Which ESG aspect is at stake?
o: Sprint velocity of the app team
Capacity is technical, not about public trust.
Right. ESG includes how projects affect the company's image and trust.
Cost isn't the issue; how the data use looks to the public is.

q.q: A contractor needs to work on a restricted network for the project. What should be confirmed first?
o: The contractor has the required screening or clearance
Right. Operational security checks people before access.
That the contractor has a personal laptop
Personal devices may not be allowed.
That the contractor can work weekends during the cutover
The contractor's hourly rate is approved
Cost matters, but access to a restricted network needs screening first.

q.q: Project documents include sensitive network diagrams. Who should be able to open them?
o: Only people with a need to know
Right. Need to know limits sensitive data to those who require it.

q.q: A team member's laptop with project files is stolen. Which control would most limit the damage?
o: Right. The data can't be read without the key.
A cable lock that came with the laptop bag
The laptop was already stolen; a lock doesn't protect the data on it.
A nightly backup of the laptop to the file server
Backups keep a copy, but the thief can still read the stolen disk.

q.q: Remote team members connect to project systems. Which control most improves digital security for their logins?
o: Right. A stolen password alone isn't enough.
A VPN connection for every remote login
A VPN protects the connection, not the login itself.
Longer and more complex passwords that change every 30 days
Passwords alone can still be phished or reused.

q.q: A project will store patients' medical records. Which type of data is this?
o: Right. Health data tied to a person is PHI and has strict rules.

q.q: A project collects customers' names, home addresses and dates of birth. Which term covers this data?
o: Personal data isn't public by default.
PHI is health-related; this is general personal data.
Right. Data that identifies a person is PII.

q.q: A project will serve users in several countries and U.S. states. What should the PM check early?
o: Nothing, since privacy laws are the same everywhere
Only the laws of the country where the company has its headquarters
Privacy laws in each country and state where data is collected
Right. Rules differ by location and affect design.
Only the vendor's terms of service
Laws apply regardless of vendor terms.

q.q: Who should the PM involve when unsure whether a requirement meets legal and regulatory rules?
o: Right. They interpret rules for the organization.
Nobody; guess and fix it later

q.q: A project replaces several separate systems for finance, HR and purchasing with one integrated suite. What type of software is this?
o: Right. ERP integrates core business processes.

q.q: A team rents virtual servers from a provider but manages the operating systems itself. Which model is this?
o: The servers are rented from a provider.
Right. The provider supplies infrastructure; the customer runs the OS and up.
PaaS manages the OS for you.

q.q: An app has a web tier, an application tier and a database tier on separate servers. What is this called?
o: Right. Splitting into tiers separates roles.
Everything would be on one system.

q.q: The sales team wants to track every customer interaction in one system. What software should the project deliver?
o: ERP covers finance, HR and supply chain.
Right. CRM tracks customers, contacts and interactions.
A ticketing system for IT only

q.q: A database upgrade will cause downtime. When should it be done?
o: Whenever the engineer is free, as long as a ticket is opened
Only after it fails in production
During an approved maintenance window, with users notified ahead
Right. Planned windows and notice reduce disruption.
At midday on a busy weekday with no notice

q.q: A change goes wrong during the maintenance window. What should already exist?
o: Right. Rollback returns systems to the last good state.

q.q: Why do teams test changes in a staging environment before production?
o: To catch problems in a copy of production without affecting users
Right. Staging mirrors production for safe testing.
Because staging hardware is faster, so tests finish sooner

q.q: After a change is made, what confirms it worked?
o: Closing the ticket as soon as the change is applied
Right. Testing after the change confirms success.
Asking the engineer if it feels fine

q.title: Order the handling of a scope change request
q.scenario: Your waterfall project has a signed baseline (the approved scope, schedule and budget). A department head emails asking you to add a second server room to the build. Your organization uses a change control board (CCB), a group that approves or rejects changes. The CCB approves the change. Put the steps in the order you would follow. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: CR-0042: add server room B to the cabling scope. Requested by email; no form filed yet.

rules.text: Record the request in the change log
rules.why: Every request gets a log entry so it cannot be lost or quietly acted on. The log also shows its status at any time.

rules.text: Do a preliminary review: is it complete, in scope of the process, not a duplicate?
rules.why: A quick screen stops the team from spending analysis time on a request that is unclear or already handled.

rules.text: Analyze the effect on scope, schedule, cost, risk and quality
rules.why: The board can only decide well when it knows what the change would cost in time, money and risk.

rules.text: Take the request and its impact analysis to the CCB for a decision
rules.why: The CCB is the group with authority to approve or reject. It needs the impact numbers in front of it.

rules.text: Update the schedule, budget and baseline to include the approved change
rules.why: The new baseline replaces the old one only after approval. Updating earlier would plan work nobody authorized.

rules.text: Send the CCB decision and the updated baseline to stakeholders and the team
rules.why: People need the new plan to work from. It can only be sent once the plans have been updated.

rules.text: Close the request in the change log after the change is built and checked
rules.why: The entry is closed only when the change is delivered and verified, so the log shows the true final status. It is the last step.

rules.text: Start long-lead cabling orders for server room B now, since approval is likely
rules.why: Spending before approval commits money to scope nobody has authorized. If the CCB says no, the orders are waste.

rules.text: Treat it as a small change and let the team lead approve it
rules.why: Changes to the baseline need the authority named in the change process, here the CCB. A team lead approving alone bypasses the control.

rules.text: Announce to stakeholders that the change is approved before the CCB meets
rules.why: Promising an outcome the board has not decided damages trust and may have to be reversed.

before.why: The review needs a logged request to work on, and logging first guarantees the request is tracked.
Do not spend analysis effort on a request that fails the first screen.
The CCB decides using the impact analysis, so it must exist before the meeting.
Plans change only after the board has approved the change.
The message to stakeholders carries the new baseline, so the baseline must be updated first.

last.why: Closing happens after the change is built and checked, so the log shows its true final status.

q.title: Place stakeholders on the power/interest grid
q.scenario: You are mapping stakeholders for a new ship-to-shore messaging app. The grid plots power (ability to change or stop the project) against interest (how much the project affects them or how much they care). Place each person in the box where they belong. Two items in the tray should not be placed.
q.ticket: Stakeholder register draft 1, reviewed with the sponsor.

slots.label: Top right
slots.hint: upper right box of the grid

slots.label: Top left
slots.hint: upper left box of the grid

slots.label: Bottom right
slots.hint: lower right box of the grid

slots.label: Bottom left
slots.hint: lower left box of the grid

devs.name: Budget owner, asks weekly
devs.why: This person controls the money and follows the work closely, so power and interest are both high. Manage closely and involve them in decisions.

devs.name: Regional CIO, can veto, rarely asks
devs.why: A regional CIO who can veto the rollout but rarely asks about it has high power and low interest. Keep satisfied with short, timely updates.

devs.name: Trainer, must teach it, no say
devs.why: A trainer has no say over scope but is strongly affected because they must teach the tool. Low power, high interest: keep informed and use their feedback.

devs.name: Facilities clerk, no say, unaffected
devs.why: A facilities clerk has no say and is not affected, so power and interest are both low. Monitor with minimal effort.

devs.name: Former sponsor, retired in May
devs.why: A person who has left has no power over or stake in the project, so they should be removed from the register rather than placed.

devs.name: Archived 2019 project team
devs.why: A finished, archived team no longer has power over or a stake in this project. It is not a stakeholder to place on the grid.

q.title: Flag work packages outside tolerance
q.scenario: This is the monthly status report for a radio rack upgrade. PV is planned value, EV is earned value (the budgeted value of work actually done) and AC is actual cost. Cost variance is CV = EV - AC. Schedule variance is SV = EV - PV. The project's rule: flag any work package whose CV or SV is more than 10% of its PV away from zero, in either direction. Mark the lines to flag, then pick the best action.
q.ticket: Report period: month 4. All amounts in dollars.

lines.text: WP1 Rack install | PV 40,000 | EV 38,000 | AC 40,000
WP2 Cable pull | PV 30,000 | EV 24,000 | AC 25,000
lines.why: CV is -1,000, which is fine, but SV is 24,000 - 30,000 = -6,000. The limit is 3,000, so the schedule is outside tolerance (behind).

lines.text: WP3 Server migration | PV 60,000 | EV 60,000 | AC 72,000
lines.why: SV is 0 but CV is 60,000 - 72,000 = -12,000. The limit is 6,000, so it is over budget and outside tolerance.
CV is +500 and SV is 0. The limit is 1,000, so a small underspend is inside tolerance.

lines.text: WP5 Acceptance testing | PV 20,000 | EV 21,000 | AC 20,000
lines.why: CV is +1,000 and SV is +1,000. The limit is 2,000, so both are inside.

lines.text: WP6 Site survey | PV 15,000 | EV 18,000 | AC 12,000
lines.why: CV is +6,000 and SV is +3,000 against a limit of 1,500. This looks like good news but is outside tolerance in the other direction. Look for the cause, such as padded estimates or work that was counted early.
CV is 50,000 - 52,000 = -2,000 and SV is 0. The limit is 5,000, so it is inside. Spending a little more than planned is not a flag by itself.

ask.label: Best next action for the project manager
opts: Take no action because the total CV of -9,500 is small next to the total PV of 225,000
Raise the limit to 20% of PV so that the report shows no exceptions
Move budget from the other packages to WP3 and say nothing about WP2 or WP6
Open variance reviews for the three flagged packages and report them to the sponsor
ask.why: Each flagged package needs a cause and a corrective or updated plan, and the sponsor should hear about exceptions. Netting them against the project total, widening the limit or moving money quietly would defeat the control.

q.title: Fill in the RACI for one task
q.scenario: A RACI chart names who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the result and signs off; only one person), Consulted (gives input before work is done) and Informed (told afterward). The task is: install the new mail gateway. Place each person in the right column. Two items in the tray should not be used.
q.ticket: Network engineer configures; director has final say; security officer's review can change the design; help desk gets the go-live notice.

slots.label: R
slots.hint: first column of the RACI row

slots.label: A
slots.hint: second column of the RACI row

slots.label: C
slots.hint: third column of the RACI row

slots.label: I
slots.hint: fourth column of the RACI row

devs.name: Network engineer
devs.why: The engineer configures the gateway, so this person does the hands-on work. That is the Responsible role.

devs.name: IT director
devs.why: The person with final say on the result is Accountable. There must be only one A per task.

devs.name: Security officer
devs.why: A review that can change the design happens before the work is final, and input flows both ways. That is Consulted.

devs.name: Help desk lead
devs.why: The help desk only gets the go-live notice afterward. One-way information after the fact is Informed.

devs.name: Deputy director
devs.why: Nothing in the ticket gives the deputy any role on this task, and the director already holds the only Accountable seat. A second sign-off would blur ownership.

devs.name: Project sponsor, funds work
devs.why: Funding the project does not give a role in this task. The ticket names no work, input or notice for the sponsor, so this person is left off the row.

q.title: Place each card on the task board
q.scenario: An agile team's task board has five columns from left to right: Backlog, Ready, In progress, In test, Done. Team rules: Ready means sized with acceptance criteria agreed; In test means coding is finished and it is with QA or waiting for product owner acceptance; Done means the product owner accepted it. Cancelled cards are not kept on the board. Put each card in the column where it belongs today. Two cards should be taken off the board.

devs.name: Sized, but no criteria yet
devs.why: It is missing acceptance criteria, so it fails the team's Ready rule. It stays in the backlog until the criteria are agreed.

devs.name: Sized, criteria agreed, next up
devs.why: It meets the team's Ready rule but nobody has started it yet.

devs.name: Developer coding it today
devs.why: Work is under way, so it belongs in the In progress column.

devs.name: Passed QA, owner not reviewed
devs.why: Testing is finished, but the product owner has not accepted it, so it is not Done. It stays in the test column until acceptance.

devs.name: Accepted by the product owner
devs.why: Acceptance is this team's rule for Done.

devs.name: Twin of a card already in progress
devs.why: A duplicate would count the same work twice. Merge it into the original and remove it from the board.

devs.name: Dropped by the product owner
devs.why: Cancelled work does not belong in any column on this team's board. Remove it and record the decision.

q.title: Order a patch change in a maintenance window
q.scenario: A patch for the unit's time-and-attendance database server must go in during the approved maintenance window, Saturday 0100 to 0300, when few people use it. Your organization uses a formal change process. Put the steps in order. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: Change 2291: patch the time-and-attendance database server. Outage expected during the window.

rules.text: Define the requirement and assess the risk of the patch
rules.why: The team needs to know why the change is needed and what could go wrong before asking for approval.

rules.text: Write the rollback plan and the validation checks
rules.why: A rollback plan returns the system to its last good state. Validation checks prove the patch works. Approvers want both before agreeing.

rules.text: Get the change approved by the change approver
rules.why: Nothing goes into production without authorization. Approval relies on the risk assessment and rollback plan.

rules.text: Tell users about the outage and its times
rules.why: People can plan around a known outage. A notice is a standard part of the process.

rules.text: Take a backup of the database at the start of the window
rules.why: If the patch and the rollback both fail, the backup is the recovery source. It must exist before the system is changed.

rules.text: Apply the patch inside the window
rules.why: The change is made only in the time the business agreed to.

rules.text: Run the validation checks and confirm the service is working
rules.why: Checks show whether to keep the change or roll back. Without them a broken patch can sit unnoticed.

rules.text: Close the change record with the result
rules.why: Closing the record documents the outcome for later audit. It follows a successful check.

rules.text: Apply the patch first and write a rollback plan only if it fails
rules.why: A plan written during a failure is slow and untested. The plan must exist before the change.

rules.text: Apply the patch at 0300 so the work is finished as the window closes
rules.why: Starting at the end of the window leaves no time to validate or roll back inside it. The patch must start early enough to be checked and reversed in the window.

rules.text: Skip validation because the patch passed in the test lab
rules.why: A lab is not production. The live system can differ, so it still has to be checked.

before.why: Approvers weigh the risk, so it must be assessed first.
The approver needs the rollback plan to know a failure can be recovered.
No change to production without approval.
Users must know before the outage begins.
The backup must be taken before the system is changed.
There is nothing to validate until the patch has been applied.
The outage notice goes out once the change is approved, not on a request that might be rejected.
No work on the production system, even a backup run, starts before approval.

last.why: The record is closed only after the result is known.
